lessons.title: Money in and money out: understanding your pay
lessons.html:
Where your money comes from

Most farm workers and poultry workers get paid every week, every two weeks or every month. The money you earn is called your income. Some people also get money from other places, like a child support grant, a small vegetable garden or selling eggs or chickens on the side. All of this is income.

Your payslip

Your employer must give you a payslip each time you are paid. Read it carefully. It shows:

  • Gross pay – the full amount you earned before anything is taken off. This includes normal hours and overtime.
  • Deductions – money taken off. Examples are UIF (Unemployment Insurance Fund), tax (PAYE) if you earn enough, and sometimes housing, a funeral policy or a loan you agreed to.
  • Net pay – the money you actually get in your hand or bank account. This is the amount you can plan with.

Check that the hours on the payslip match the hours you worked. If something looks wrong, ask your supervisor or the farm office politely. Keep your payslips in a safe place. You will need them to open a bank account, apply for credit or claim UIF.

Where your money goes

Money that you spend is called an expense. Some expenses come every month and stay about the same, like rent, school fees, a funeral policy, or taxi fare to town. These are fixed expenses. Other expenses change, like food, airtime, electricity and clothes. These are changing or variable expenses.

Needs and wants

A need is something you must have to live and work: food, shelter, water, electricity, transport to work, school costs for children. A want is something nice to have but you can live without it, like a new phone, takeaways or a new TV. Pay for needs first. Spend on wants only when the needs are covered.

A simple exercise: for one month, write down every rand you spend in a small book. At the end of the month, add up each group (food, transport, airtime, and so on). Many people are surprised to see how much small things, like cold drinks and airtime, cost over a month.

lessons.title: Making a budget that works
lessons.html:
What is a budget?

A budget is a plan for your money. It shows how much money comes in and how you will use it. A budget helps you to pay for your needs, to avoid running out of money before payday and to save for the future.

Steps to make a monthly budget

  1. Write down your net pay for the month and any other income.
  2. List your fixed expenses (rent, funeral policy, school fees, transport).
  3. List your changing expenses and guess a fair amount for each (food, electricity, airtime).
  4. Put an amount aside for savings, even if it is small.
  5. Add up all the expenses and savings. Take this away from your income.
  6. If the answer is less than zero, you are spending more than you earn. Cut back on wants first.

Example: Thandi's budget

Thandi works in a broiler house and takes home R4 800 a month.

ItemAmount
FoodR1 800
TransportR600
Electricity and airtimeR500
School costsR400
Funeral policyR200
Money sent homeR800
SavingsR300
TotalR4 600

R4 800 minus R4 600 leaves R200 for surprises. Thandi's budget balances. She can add the R200 to her savings if no surprise costs come up this month.

Tips to stick to your budget

  • Buy food in bulk at month-end with others and share, if the price per kilogram is lower.
  • Make a shopping list and stick to it.
  • Compare prices between shops.
  • Talk with your family about the budget so everyone knows the plan.
  • Look at your budget again every month. Things change, like school fees in January.

lessons.title: Saving, credit and staying out of debt trouble
lessons.html:
Why save?

Saving means keeping some money aside and not spending it now. Savings help when something unexpected happens: a sick child, a broken bicycle, or a funeral. Savings also help you reach goals, like buying building materials or paying for a child's school uniform in January.

Ways to save

  • A bank savings account – your money is safe and can earn a little interest.
  • A stokvel – a group of people who each pay in an amount every month. Choose a stokvel with people you trust, written rules and clear records.
  • Saving at home – easy to reach, but money can be stolen or spent quickly. It is safer in a bank.

Credit and loans

Credit means you buy something now and pay for it later. When you borrow money, you pay back more than you borrowed. The extra money is called interest and fees. The longer you take to pay, the more you pay in total.

Before you take credit, ask:

  • Do I really need this, or is it a want?
  • How much will I pay back in total, not just each month?
  • Can my budget carry this payment every month?

Danger signs

Never give your bank card and PIN, or your ID book, to a lender to keep. This is illegal and leaves you with no control over your money. Be very careful of loan sharks (mashonisa) who charge very high interest. Use only lenders that are registered with the National Credit Regulator. If you are struggling to pay your debts, ask for help early, for example from a debt counsellor.

Protect your money

Never share your PIN or one-time PIN (OTP) with anyone, even someone who says they are from the bank. The bank will never ask for it. Count your money at the ATM and keep your slip.

Key points

  • Net pay is the money you can actually plan with.
  • Pay for needs before wants.
  • A budget compares money in with money out every month.
  • Save a little every month, even a small amount.
  • Credit costs more than the price because of interest and fees.
  • Never hand over your bank card, PIN or ID to a lender.
